source.title: Evaluating Language Model Safety Across Long Adversarial Conversations

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or wrong-document issue. Some tables and figures are flattened in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests safety-response rates during sustained multi-turn adversarial interaction, a related extension not covered by the listed claim versions’ specific fine-tuning or token-depth interventions.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmful-request safe-response rates across conversation depth. It does not fine-tune models, measure aligned-versus-base KL across response positions, or test compliant prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, safety-localized parameters, causes of token shallowness, or deepening interventions. The rates are cataloged under fits_no_version because they do not test a listed version’s specified intervention or mechanism. Related-work results cited by the paper are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures how safe-response rates of fixed instruction-tuned models decline under a persistent LLM-simulated adversarial user over 11 and 101 turns. It involves no fine-tuning (V1, V2) and no per-token KL (V3). It uses no compliant prefill, suffix or decoding change (V4); the authors stress the decline occurred 'without adversarial suffixes, encoded prompts, persona manipulation'. It has no parameter localization (V5), no cause of shallowness (V6) and no deepening training (V7). Qi et al. (the second original source) appears only in the reference list. The record's 'tests'/T3 contradicts its own finding that no version is tested, so this is relabelled cites_only/T6. The multi-turn decline is a related but different construct and stays under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also interpret the assistant/shadow-user divergence (Fig. 5) as consistent with a history-dependent process. They caution that it does not show accumulated context is the sole cause, and that their design cannot separate repetition, depth, user context and prior assistant responses.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates fixed instruction-tuned models in automated multi-turn adversarial conversations; it does not fine-tune, edit model weights, or measure response-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported rates vary by model, harmful prompt, and conversation depth; the study also notes that rates depend partly on the fixed safety classifier.

fits_no_version.finding: Across all three models and both prompts, Llama-Guard-4 safe-response rates fell between turns. They went from 0.85–1.00 at turn 1 to 0.38–0.61 at depth 11 (exhaustive trees, 10 seeds) and to 0.15–0.44 at depth 101 (2500 sampled paths per model–prompt). Assistant safety kept declining after depths 30–40 even as shadow-user messages were classified safer (Fig. 5, qualitative).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under sustained same-model adversarial persistence, instruction-tuned models' refusal of a fixed harmful request erodes with conversation depth, consistent with a history-dependent process rather than increasing per-turn prompt harmfulness.

record.code_released: The authors state that methodology and aggregate results are released, but no URL is stated.
record.problems: The study covers only two harmful prompts and uses one automated safety classifier; alternative classifiers and human reviewers were left for future work. The authors say the design cannot separate repetition, turn depth, accumulated user context, and previous assistant responses, and does not isolate a cause for degradation. The paper describes the work as proof of concept.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 1–4 show additional depth- or seed-level plots, and Figure 5 describes diverging assistant and shadow-user safety trends; these were not separately extracted because the text does not provide corresponding model-specific numeric values. The aggregate table results are included in rows r1–r12.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning; models are explicitly not fine-tuned.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes. The study's multi-turn persistence is a different attack, not a bypass of the response opening.
Localization of safety in weights or ranks.
Data or objective causes of shallow alignment.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are accurate against Tables I and II. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The text mentions a 'comparison of full-context and turn-local scoring' as an initial judge check but reports no numbers for it. The adversary is the same model in a different role, so the attack is model-generated multi-turn pressure, not a prefill. Only two undisclosed prompts and one classifier were used; the paper is a proof of concept.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes as bypass methods.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety and whether deepened safety holds up.
